'''Richard Dale Smith''' is a [[chemist]] and a [[Battelle Memorial Institute|Battelle]] Fellow and chief scientist within the biological sciences division, as well as the director of proteomics research at the [[Pacific Northwest National Laboratory]] (PNNL). Smith is also director of the [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] Proteomics Research Resource for Integrative Biology, an adjunct faculty member in the chemistry departments at [[Washington State University]] and the [[University of Utah]], and an affiliate faculty member at the [[University of Idaho]] and the Department of Molecular Microbiology & Immunology, [[Oregon Health & Science University]].<ref name=PNNL>{{cite web |url= http://www.pnl.gov/science/staff/staff_info.asp?staff_num=5832|title= Richard D. Smith}}</ref> He is the author or co-author of approximately 1100 peer-reviewed publications and has been awarded 70 US patents.<ref name=Planet>{{cite web | url=http://planetorbitrap.com/richard-smith#.UuaO47Dn_IV | title=Focus on Richard D. Smith, PhD | publisher=Thermo Fisher}}</ref>

==Education==
Smith obtained his B.S. in chemistry in 1971 from [[Lowell Technological Institute]] (currently the [[University of Massachusetts Lowell]]).<ref name=PNNL /><ref name=PNNLNews>{{cite web |url=http://www.pnl.gov/news/release.aspx?id=586 | title=Smith Named Inventor of the Year | publisher=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory}}</ref> He then received his PhD in the field of [[Physical Chemistry]] from the [[University of Utah]] in 1975.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pnl.gov/science/staff/staff_info.asp?staff_num=5832|title=Richard Smith, Ph.D}}</ref>

==Early career==
Starting in the 1970s Smith published peer-reviewed papers on several subjects, including [[mass spectrometry]], ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry, ion-molecule reactions, molecular assemblies, and [[supercritical fluid]] solutions.<ref>{{cite journal |title= Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry with Electron Impact and Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry with a Ribbon Storage Interface|journal = Analytical Chemistry|volume = 53|issue = 11|last1=Smith|first1=R.D.|last2=Burger|first2=J.E.|last3=Johnson|first3=A.L.|year=1981|pages=1603–1611|doi= 10.1021/ac00234a016}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title= Capillary Column Supercritical Fluid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry|journal = Analytical Chemistry|volume = 54|issue = 11|last1=Smith|first1=R. D.|last2=Fjeldsted|first2=J. C.|last3=Lee|first3=M. T.|last4=Felix|first4=W.D.|year=1982|pages=1883–1885|doi= 10.1021/ac00248a055}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title= Organized Molecular Assemblies in the Gas Phase: Reverse Micelles and Microemulsions in Supercritical Fluids|journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume = 109|issue = 3|last1=Gale|first1=R. W.|last2=Fulton|first2=J. L.|last3=Smith|first3=R. D.|year=1987|pages=920–921|doi= 10.1021/ja00237a059}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Matson|first1=D.W.|last2=Petersen|first2=R.C.|last3=Smith|first3=R.D.|title=Formation of Silica Powders from the Rapid Expansion of Supercritical Fluid Solutions|publisher=Advanced Ceramic Materials|year=1986|pages=242–246}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title= Rapid Precipitation of Low Vapor Pressure Solids from Supercritical Fluid Solutions: The Formation of Thin Films and Powders|journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume = 108|issue = 8|last1=Matson|first1=D.W.|last2=Petersen|first2=R.C.|last3=Smith|first3=R.D.|year=1986|pages=2100–2102|doi= 10.1021/ja00268a066}}</ref>  This early work has led him to be considered an internationally recognized expert in mass spectrometry and separation techniques, and his research has led to advancements in instrumentation for the medical and environmental analysis fields, as well as biological research.<ref name=PNNLNews2>{{cite web | url=http://www.pnl.gov/news/release.aspx?id=586|title=Smith named Inventor of the Year|date=March 21, 2000|publisher=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory}}</ref>

In the medical field, Smith's work has produced benefits in the areas of drug testing, analysis of pharmaceuticals and medical diagnostics in the clinical arena. His most successful invention has been the combination of capillary electro-phoresis with mass spectrometry. By the end of the 1990s, Smith's achievements included the electrodynamic ion funnel and a micro-dialysis device for the rapid purification of samples analyzed using mass spectrometry. Other notable contributions have been in the fields of supercritical fluids and related reverse micelle phenomena.

On August 22, 2000, Smith demonstrated and patented<ref>"Method and Apparatus for Directing Ions and Other Charged Particles Generated at Near Atmospheric Pressure into a Region under Vacuum," issued August 22, 2000, to R. D. Smith and S. A. Shaffer, U. S. Patent No. 6,107,628.</ref> the electrodynamic ion funnel<ref>{{cite journal |title= A Novel Ion Funnel for Focusing Ions at Elevated Pressure Using Electrospray Ionization Mass Spectrometry|last1=Shaffer|first1=S. A.|last2=Tang|first2=K.|last3=Anderson|first3=G. A.|last4=Prior|first4=D. C.|last5=Udseth|first5=H. R.|last6=Smith|first6=R. D. |pages=1813–1817|date=October 30, 1997|doi=10.1002/(SICI)1097-0231(19971030)11:16<1813::AID-RCM87>3.0.CO;2-D|volume=11|issue = 16|journal=Rapid Communications in Mass Spectrometry}}</ref><ref name=PNNLNews3>{{cite web | url=http://www.pnl.gov/science/highlights/highlight.asp?id=839|title=Award-Winning Ion Funnel Technology Gets Another License|publisher=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory}}</ref> for highly efficient capture and focusing of ions in gases. He applied it for increasing the sensitivity of ESI-MS.<ref>{{cite journal |title= An Ion Funnel Interface for Improved Ion Focusing and Sensitivity Using Electrospray Ionization Mass Spectrometry|journal = Analytical Chemistry|volume = 70|issue = 19|last1=Shaffer|first1=S. A.|last2=Prior|first2=D. C.|last3=Anderson|first3=G. A.|last4=Udseth|first4=H. R.|last5=Smith|first5=R.D.|year=1998|pages=4111–4119|doi= 10.1021/ac9802170|pmid = 9784749}}</ref> His group has continued to refine and extend ion funnel technology, which is now widely applied in mass spectrometry and ion mobility instrumentation.<ref name=PNNLNews3 /><ref>{{cite journal|title=The Ion Funnel:Theory, Implementations and Applications|last1=Kelly|first1=R.T.|last2=Tolmachev|first2=A.V.|last3=Page|first3=J.S.|last4=Tang|first4=K.|last5=Smith|first5=R.D.|journal=Mass Spectrometry Reviews|publisher=Mass Spectrometry|year=2010|volume=29|issue=2|pages=294–312|doi=10.1002/mas.20232|pmid=19391099|pmc=2824015|bibcode=2010MSRv...29..294K }}</ref>

In the late 1990s, Smith's group was also extensively involved in the development and application of [[Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance]] (FTICR) mass spectrometry, which provided the basis for much greater MS resolution and mass measurement accuracy, and particularly in the development of these technologies for applications in [[proteomics]].<ref name=PNNLNews5>{{cite web |url=http://www.pnnl.gov/biology/research/separations.stm|title=MS&D: Biological Separations and Mass Spectrometry|publisher=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=High Resolution Accurate Mass Measurements of Biomolecules Using a Novel Electrospray Ionization Ion Cyclotron Resonance Mass Spectrometer|journal=Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry|volume=4|issue=7|last1=Winger|first1=B. E.|last2=Hofstadler|first2=S. A.|last3=Bruce|first3=J. E.|last4=Udseth|first4=H. R.|last5=Smith|first5=R. D.|year=1993|pages=566–577|doi=10.1016/1044-0305(93)85018-S|pmid = 24227643|doi-access=|s2cid=34574050 }}</ref> More recent work has centered on extending application of these proteomics technologies to mammalian systems, which pose additional challenges due to their much greater complexity. One early focus has been the human blood plasma proteome due to its broad biomedical applications. Plasma proteome measurements potentially can provide the basis for discovery of protein biomarkers or signatures for virtually every disease state.<ref name=PNNLNews5 />

In September 1999, ''R&D Magazine'' picked the top 40 technologies of all time based on their impact on society, industry and commercial applications. The Top 40 were selected from a list of 3,600 past R&D 100 Awards. Smith was the recipient of one of these awards, for the development of [[capillary electrophoresis-mass spectrometry]].<ref name=PNNLNews2 />

==Current research==
Since the [[Human Genome Project]] developed a blueprint of all human genes in our chromosomes, proteomics researchers have pushed to understand how that blueprint creates life. Diseases and infections are often the result of proteins going wrong, and finding the aberrant one requires sifting through thousands of other proteins. In addition, many problem proteins have not been given names yet or are too rare to find easily.

In the last few years, Smith and his team have led work that has reduced analytical steps from hours to minutes. This increased speed has enabled many samples to be processed faster in high-throughput experiments. Smith has led other advances in sensitivity and accuracy that have improved the ability to find rare proteins, bringing proteomics technology to the doorstep of clinical researchers.

Smith and collaborators have applied the technology to liver disease and cancer in the hopes of finding rare markers of disease in blood, making diagnosis or treatment safer and faster. In 2007, Scientific American magazine listed Smith and his collaborator Desmond Smith as one of the top 50 researchers for work to understand the origins of Parkinson's disease by mapping where proteins amass in diseased mouse brains.

Among other work, Smith and colleagues at PNNL looked at how bacteria and viruses might cause illness. They've learned breast cancer leaves traces in the blood that doctors might research on someday. Smith led early studies for DOE into possible roles for microbes in making biofuels. In other DOE studies, he's examined how large environmental communities of microbes function in our ecosystem and affect our environment.<ref name=PNNLNews1>{{cite web | url=http://www.pnl.gov/news/release.aspx?id=829 | title=PNNL's Richard Smith named 2010 Scientist of the Year | publisher=Pacific Northwest National Laboratory|date=October 25, 2013}}</ref>

In other recent work he has been leading the development of [[structures for lossless ion manipulations]] (SLIM) and their application for very high speed sample processing, reactions, separations, and other manipulations of ions in the gas phase, and particularly their use for ion mobility spectrometry (IMS) separations in conjunction with mass spectrometry. Smith and colleagues at PNNL, including Drs. Yehia Ibrahim and Sandilya Gerimella, have extended the range of SLIM technologies to include the use of travel wave electric fields for SLIM IMS.  This has enabled extremely high resolution separations based on 'multi-pass" separations, and has enabled the separation of ions previously impractical, such as isotopomers and isotopologues.

==Awards and affiliations==
Smith a principal investigator at [[NIH]] Biomedical Technology Resource Center for [[Integrative Biology]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nigms.nih.gov/About/Overview/BBCB/BiomedicalTechnology/BiomedicalTechnologyResearchCenters.htm|title=National Institute of General Medical Sciences|access-date=2012-10-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121027110616/http://www.nigms.nih.gov/About/Overview/BBCB/BiomedicalTechnology/BiomedicalTechnologyResearchCenters.htm|archive-date=2012-10-27}}</ref> and the [[U.S. Department of Energy]] High Throughput Proteomics Facility at PNNL.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dac.neu.edu/barnett/BInews_2009/smithlecture.htm|title= Department of Energy High Throughput Proteomics Facility}}</ref> He is an adjunct faculty member in the chemistry departments at Washington State University and the University of Utah and an affiliate faculty member Department of Chemistry at the University of Idaho and the Department of Molecular Microbiology & Immunology, Oregon Health & Science University.  Smith serves on the Board of Scientific Counselors,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/phpr/science/members_exofficios.htm|title=Board of Scientific Counselors Membership List}}</ref> Office of Public Health Preparedness and Response of the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]]. He is also a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.membercentral.aaas.org/fellows|title=AAAS Fellows}}</ref> and has been elected to the Washington State Academy of Sciences.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.washacad.org/members/index.html|title=Washington State Academy of Sciences Membership}}</ref>

In 2011, ''[[Discover Magazine]]'' selected a peer-reviewed paper on [[Lyme disease]] that he coauthored with [[immunologist]] Steven Schutzer of the [[University of Medicine and Dentistry of New Jersey]] as one of the top 100 articles of the year, placing it at number 90.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://discovermagazine.com/2012/jan-feb/90#.UVnrdFccM3U|title=Discover Magazine: #90: Chronic Lyme Patients Validated }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title= Distinct Cerebrospinal Fluid Proteomes Differentiate Post-Treatment Lyme Disease from Chronic Fatigue Syndrome |journal=PLOS ONE|volume=6|issue=2|article-number=e17287|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0017287|year = 2011|last1 = Schutzer|first1 = Steven E.|last2=Angel|first2=Thomas E.|last3=Liu|first3=Tao|last4=Schepmoes|first4=Athena A.|last5=Clauss|first5=Therese R.|last6=Adkins|first6=Joshua N.|last7=Camp|first7=David G.|last8=Holland|first8=Bart K.|last9=Bergquist|first9=Jonas|last10=Coyle|first10=Patricia K.|last11=Smith|first11=Richard D.|last12=Fallon|first12=Brian A.|last13=Natelson|first13=Benjamin H.|pmc=3044169|pmid=21383843|bibcode=2011PLoSO...617287S|doi-access=free}}</ref> 
He was the recipient of the 2003 ACS award in Analytical Chemistry,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://webapps.acs.org/findawards/detail.jsp?ContentId=CTP_004492|title=ACS Award in Analytical Chemistry|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111005204036/http://webapps.acs.org/findawards/detail.jsp?ContentId=CTP_004492|archive-date=2011-10-05}}</ref> the 2009 [[Human Proteome Organization]] (HUPO) Discovery Award in Proteomics Sciences, and was selected by ''R&D Magazine'' as the 2010 R&D Scientist of the Year.<ref name=PNNLNews1 />  He has also received ten R&D 100 Awards: Combined Orthogonal Mobility & Mass Evaluation Technology (2013); Ion Mobility Spectrometer on a Microchip (2010); Ultrasensitive Electrospray Ionization Mass Spectrometry Source and Interface (2009);  FT-MS Proteome Express (2003); Electrodynamic Ion Funnel (1999); Rapid Microdialyzer (1998); MICLEAN/MICARE Process (1998); Rapid Expansion of Supercritical Fluid Solutions Process (1988); Capillary Electrophoresis-Electrospray Ionization-MS (1988); and  Supercritical Fluid Chromatography-MS (1983).  He was the recipient of the 2013 Award for a Distinguished Contribution in Mass Spectrometry.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Focus on Advancing High Performance Mass Spectrometry, Honoring Dr. Richard D. Smith, Recipient of the 2013 Award for a Distinguished Contribution in Mass Spectrometry|journal=Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry|volume=25|issue=12|pages=1997–1999|doi=10.1007/s13361-014-1007-8|pmid=25326057|year = 2014|last1 = Baker|first1 = Erin S.|last2=Muddiman|first2=David C.|last3=Loo|first3=Joseph A.|bibcode=2014JASMS..25.1997B|doi-access=free}}</ref>
